title: Oscillating Through Grief
text:
For much of the twentieth century, a common view held that the bereaved must do "grief work": confront the loss directly and work through painful feelings, or risk trouble later. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, bereavement researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, found that the evidence for this view was weaker than its popularity suggested, and that it did not fit what many grieving people actually did.

In 1999 they published the dual process model of coping with bereavement. They described two kinds of stress after a death. Loss-oriented coping deals with the loss itself: crying, yearning, looking at photographs, thinking about the person who died. Restoration-oriented coping deals with the life that remains: learning to handle the finances the spouse used to manage, building new routines, taking on new roles, and sometimes simply taking a break from grief by watching television or seeing friends.

The key idea was oscillation. Healthy grieving, they argued, does not mean staying in one mode. People move back and forth, sometimes within a single day, confronting the loss and then turning away from it. Too much of either can cause problems. The model has since become one of the most widely used frameworks in bereavement research and counseling.
lesson: When you or someone you love is grieving, it is fine to step away from sorrow to handle daily life or even enjoy a moment. Both belong to mourning.
source: Stroebe, M., and Schut, H. (1999). The dual process model of coping with bereavement: Rationale and description. Death Studies, 23(3), 197-224.
caveat: This is a theoretical model built on earlier research rather than a single experiment, and evidence testing it directly is still limited.
